title: Calcium and Alcohol: Absorption, Bone Health, and Safe Timing
excerpt: Can you take calcium with alcohol? How drinking affects calcium absorption and bone health, how much calcium you need, which form to choose, and signs of low calcium.
metaDescription: Can you take calcium with alcohol? How drinking affects calcium absorption and bones, how much you need, which form to pick, and signs of low calcium.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most healthy adults, taking a normal calcium supplement and having a few drinks is not a dangerous combination. The more important story runs the other way. **Regular heavy drinking disrupts how your body absorbs, uses, and stores calcium**, and over years that can thin your bones and raise your risk of fractures. One night out won't do that to a well-fed person. A pattern of heavy drinking can. This guide explains how alcohol affects calcium, whether you can take a calcium supplement with or after drinking, how much calcium you actually need, which form to choose, and the signs that mean you should see a doctor.

**The quick rules:** It's generally fine to take calcium on a day you drink. Take it with food and water, ideally after you have stopped drinking, and stick to the label dose. Most adults need 1,000 to 1,200 mg a day from food and supplements combined, and food is the best source. Calcium can block the absorption of some common medicines, including certain antibiotics and thyroid medicine, so space them apart. If you take prescription medicine, have kidney problems, or have had kidney stones, talk to your doctor or pharmacist first. And there is no good evidence that calcium prevents or cures a hangover.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes general research and official nutrition guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before taking calcium supplements if** you have kidney disease, a history of kidney stones, a parathyroid condition, high blood calcium, or take prescription medicines (especially antibiotics, thyroid medicine, osteoporosis drugs, heart medicines, or diuretics). If you're worried about your drinking or your bone health, a doctor can check your vitamin D, calcium, and bone density.

## How Alcohol Affects Calcium: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Calcium isn't just for bones, although that's where about 99% of it lives. The small amount in your blood keeps your heart beating steadily, lets your muscles contract and relax, and helps nerves send signals. Your body guards that blood level closely. When it starts to drop, a hormone from your parathyroid glands (small glands in your neck) pulls calcium out of your bones to keep the blood level steady. That works fine in the short term. Over years, constantly borrowing from your bones weakens them.

Alcohol interferes with this system at several points.

### 1. You may absorb less calcium from food

Calcium is absorbed in your small intestine, and that process depends heavily on **vitamin D**. Your skin and diet supply vitamin D in an inactive form. Your liver and then your kidneys convert it into the active hormone that tells your gut to absorb calcium. Heavy drinking can damage the gut lining and strain the liver, and people who drink heavily often have low vitamin D levels. Less active vitamin D means less calcium gets absorbed from the same meal. Our guide to [vitamin D and alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamin-d-and-alcohol) covers that side of the picture in more detail.

### 2. Your kidneys may let more calcium go

Alcohol is a diuretic, which means it makes you urinate more. Studies going back decades have found that drinking increases the amount of calcium lost in urine for a while afterward. For a single night, the amount is small and a normal diet replaces it. For someone who drinks heavily most days, the extra losses add up.

### 3. Alcohol throws off the hormones that control calcium

Research on heavy drinking has found it can disrupt parathyroid hormone and vitamin D signaling, the two main systems that keep blood calcium in balance. Heavy drinking also tends to raise cortisol (a stress hormone that weakens bone when it stays high) and can lower testosterone in men and disrupt estrogen in women. Both sex hormones help protect bone, so changes to them add to the problem.

### 4. Low magnesium makes low calcium harder to fix

This is the part most articles skip. Alcohol also drains **magnesium**, and your parathyroid glands need magnesium to release their hormone and for that hormone to work. When magnesium is very low, blood calcium can fall and stay low even if you take calcium, until the magnesium is corrected. That's why doctors who find low calcium in heavy drinkers usually check magnesium too. Our [magnesium and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol) explains how drinking depletes it.

### 5. Alcohol directly slows bone building

Bone isn't static. Cells called osteoblasts constantly build new bone while other cells break old bone down. Lab and animal research suggests alcohol directly suppresses osteoblasts, so the building side falls behind. That means even if calcium is available, heavy drinking can still make it harder for your body to turn it into strong bone.

### What this means in practice

For a social drinker who eats reasonably well, the calcium effects of an occasional night out are temporary and minor. The real concern is **long-term heavy drinking**, where reduced absorption, increased loss, hormone changes, low magnesium and vitamin D, and slower bone building all pile up at once. Add the higher risk of falls when you're drunk, and you get the pattern seen in research: heavy drinkers have lower bone density and more fractures, especially hip fractures.

## Does Alcohol Deplete Calcium?

Yes, but how much depends almost entirely on how much and how often you drink.

- **After a single night of drinking:** your body loses a bit more calcium in urine than usual. Your blood calcium stays normal because your body tightly controls it. There's no need to "replace" calcium the next morning beyond eating normally.
- **With regular moderate drinking:** research is mixed. Some studies have found light-to-moderate drinkers have similar or even slightly higher bone density than non-drinkers, particularly in older women. That's not a reason to start drinking. Those studies are observational, meaning they can't prove cause and effect, and people who drink moderately often differ from non-drinkers in other ways.
- **With long-term heavy drinking:** calcium losses, poor absorption, and the hormone effects above are well documented. This is the pattern linked to lower bone density, osteoporosis, and fractures.

Blood tests often look normal even when the body's calcium balance is off, because your body will raid your bones to keep the blood level steady. A normal blood calcium result doesn't tell you your bones are fine. A bone density scan (a DEXA scan) is the test that does that.

## Can You Take Calcium Supplements With Alcohol?

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no known dangerous reaction between a standard calcium supplement and a few drinks. A few practical points make it work better:

- **Take it with food.** Calcium carbonate, the most common and cheapest form, needs stomach acid to dissolve and absorbs best with a meal. Taking it on an empty stomach after a night of drinking means less gets absorbed.
- **Wait until you've stopped drinking.** Alcohol can irritate the stomach and may reduce absorption. There's no benefit to taking calcium during drinking, and it's easier to remember with breakfast or dinner anyway.
- **Keep each dose to about 500 mg or less.** Your gut absorbs calcium best in smaller amounts. If you take 1,000 mg of supplements a day, split it into two doses.
- **Drink water.** You'll want to rehydrate after drinking anyway, and it helps with the constipation some people get from calcium.

Calcium won't make you less drunk, won't speed up how fast you clear alcohol, and won't protect your bones from a pattern of heavy drinking. It covers a gap in your diet. That's all.

## Taking Calcium After Drinking: Does It Help a Hangover?

There is no good evidence that calcium supplements prevent or relieve a hangover. Hangovers come from a mix of things, including dehydration, poor sleep, irritation of the stomach lining, inflammation, and the effects of acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product made when your body breaks down alcohol). Calcium doesn't address any of those directly.

Where calcium sometimes does show up in hangover routines is as **an antacid**. Tums and many store-brand antacids are calcium carbonate. If drinking leaves you with heartburn or an acid stomach, a calcium carbonate antacid can neutralize the acid and ease that symptom. It's not treating the hangover itself, just the burning. Our guide to [Tums and alcohol](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol) covers how to use antacids sensibly after drinking, and [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) explains why alcohol triggers reflux.

One caution: people who chew antacids all evening and also take a calcium supplement can end up with far more calcium than they realize. A single regular-strength Tums tablet contains a meaningful amount of calcium, and it all counts toward your daily total. Read the label and add it up.

## How Much Calcium Do You Actually Need?

The US National Institutes of Health (NIH) Office of Dietary Supplements sets these recommended daily amounts for adults, counting both food and supplements:

| Group | Recommended daily calcium | Upper limit per day |
|---|---|---|
| Adults 19 to 50 | 1,000 mg | 2,500 mg |
| Men 51 to 70 | 1,000 mg | 2,000 mg |
| Women 51 to 70 | 1,200 mg | 2,000 mg |
| Adults 71 and older | 1,200 mg | 2,000 mg |

A few things worth knowing about those numbers:

- **The goal is the total, not the supplement.** If you eat a couple of servings of dairy or fortified foods a day, you may need little or no supplement. Many people take far more supplemental calcium than they need.
- **More isn't better.** Going over the upper limit regularly raises the risk of kidney stones, constipation, and in rare cases dangerously high blood calcium.
- **Drinking doesn't change the target.** There's no official guidance telling drinkers to take extra calcium. The better move is to make sure you're actually hitting the normal target, since heavy drinkers often don't.

### Good food sources of calcium

Food is the best place to get calcium because it comes with other nutrients that help bone, and research hasn't linked dietary calcium to the concerns raised about high-dose supplements. Good sources include:

- Milk, yogurt, and cheese
- Fortified plant milks (soy, almond, oat) and fortified orange juice
- Tofu made with calcium sulfate (check the label)
- Canned sardines and canned salmon with the soft bones
- Leafy greens like kale, bok choy, and collard greens
- Broccoli, white beans, almonds, and fortified cereals

Spinach contains calcium, but it also contains oxalate, which binds calcium and blocks much of it from being absorbed. It's still a healthy food, just not a great calcium source.

## Which Form of Calcium Is Best?

The two main forms you'll find are calcium carbonate and calcium citrate.

| | Calcium carbonate | Calcium citrate |
|---|---|---|
| Calcium per tablet | Higher (about 40% calcium by weight) | Lower (about 21%), so more or bigger pills |
| Take with food? | Yes, needs stomach acid | Works with or without food |
| Cost | Usually cheaper | Usually pricier |
| Stomach side effects | More gas, bloating, constipation for some | Often gentler |
| Best for | Most people who take it with meals | People on acid-reducing medicine, older adults, people with sensitive stomachs |

**For people who drink:** if you often take your supplement the morning after drinking on an empty or upset stomach, or you take acid-reducing medicine for reflux (like omeprazole), calcium citrate is the more forgiving choice. If you reliably take it with a meal, carbonate works well and costs less.

Many calcium supplements also include vitamin D, which makes sense since you need vitamin D to absorb calcium. Some also include magnesium. Check the totals so you don't double up with other products.

## Calcium, Alcohol, and Bone Health

This is the main reason people search "calcium and alcohol," and it deserves a clear answer.

Long-term heavy drinking is a recognized risk factor for osteoporosis, a condition where bones become thin and break easily. The FRAX tool that doctors use to estimate fracture risk asks whether you drink three or more units of alcohol a day, because research has linked that level of drinking to higher fracture risk. Bone health organizations, including the Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation, recommend limiting alcohol as part of protecting your bones.

Heavy drinking harms bone in several ways at once: less calcium absorbed, more calcium lost, hormone disruption, low vitamin D and magnesium, slower bone building, and more falls. That's why **calcium supplements alone can't offset heavy drinking.** If the drinking continues, the other damage continues too.

The more encouraging news is that research on people who stop drinking heavily suggests bone building can start to recover, though it may take time and may not fully reverse long-standing damage. Cutting back helps.

For a deeper look at how alcohol affects your skeleton, including fracture risk by drinking level, see our [complete guide to alcohol and bone health](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-bone-health-complete-skeletal-impact-analysis).

### Who should pay extra attention to bone health

- **Women after menopause**, when falling estrogen speeds up bone loss
- **Men and women over 50**
- **People with a small frame or low body weight**
- **People with a family history of osteoporosis or hip fracture**
- **Anyone who has broken a bone from a minor fall**
- **People who take long-term steroid medicines**
- **People who smoke** or drink heavily

If any of these apply to you and you drink regularly, ask your doctor whether a bone density scan makes sense.

## Calcium Supplements and Medications: Interactions to Know

Calcium itself interacts with several common medicines, and that matters more than any calcium and alcohol interaction. Calcium can bind to some drugs in your gut and stop them from being absorbed. The usual fix is to take them a few hours apart, but the exact timing depends on the drug, so ask your pharmacist.

- **Certain antibiotics**, including tetracyclines (like doxycycline) and fluoroquinolones (like ciprofloxacin). Calcium can sharply reduce how much gets absorbed.
- **Levothyroxine** (thyroid medicine). Calcium can lower absorption, so it's usually taken several hours apart.
- **Osteoporosis drugs called bisphosphonates** (like alendronate). These have strict instructions about taking them on an empty stomach, apart from calcium and food.
- **Iron supplements.** Calcium can reduce iron absorption when taken at the same time.
- **Thiazide diuretics** (like hydrochlorothiazide). These reduce how much calcium your kidneys get rid of, so high-dose calcium on top can push blood calcium too high.

Several of these medicines have their own alcohol considerations as well. If you take any of them, your doctor or pharmacist is the right person to give you a schedule. Our [medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements.

## Calcium Channel Blockers and Alcohol

People also search "calcium and alcohol" when they mean a type of blood pressure and heart medicine called **calcium channel blockers**. These include amlodipine, diltiazem, nifedipine, and verapamil. They don't contain calcium. They relax blood vessels and, for some of them, slow the heart by limiting how calcium moves into muscle cells.

The main concern with alcohol is that both lower blood pressure, so together they can make you dizzy, lightheaded, or more likely to faint, especially when you stand up quickly. Verapamil has also been reported in research to slow how fast the body clears alcohol, which could mean higher blood alcohol levels for longer. On the other side, regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure, which works against the reason you're taking the medicine in the first place.

If you take a calcium channel blocker, talk to your doctor or pharmacist about whether and how much you can drink. Don't stop or skip your medicine to drink.

## Low Calcium and Alcohol: Symptoms to Know

Low blood calcium (called hypocalcemia) is uncommon in social drinkers. It's more likely in people who drink heavily for long periods, especially alongside poor eating, low magnesium, low vitamin D, or pancreatitis. Signs include:

- Tingling or numbness around the mouth or in the fingers and toes
- Muscle cramps or spasms, especially in the hands and feet
- Twitching muscles
- Fatigue and weakness
- Confusion or irritability
- In severe cases, an abnormal heart rhythm or seizures

Many of these overlap with dehydration, low magnesium, low potassium, or simply a rough hangover, so they're hard to pin on calcium without a blood test. Our guides to [potassium and alcohol](/never-hungover/potassium-and-alcohol) and [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) cover the other minerals that drinking can throw off.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most mild muscle cramps or tiredness after a night out pass within a day with water, food, and rest. Book a doctor's appointment if you have muscle cramps, twitching, or tingling that keep coming back, a bone that broke from a minor bump or fall, or you drink most days and want your vitamin D, calcium, magnesium, or bone density checked.
>
> **Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US)** if you or someone else has a seizure, severe muscle spasms that won't let go, chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, fainting, or confusion. If you drink heavily on most days and have shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or seeing things that aren't there after stopping or cutting back, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Get medical help rather than trying to manage it alone.

## Calcium Supplements, Kidney Stones, and Your Heart

Two concerns come up often with calcium supplements, and both are worth knowing about if you drink.

**Kidney stones.** The most common kidney stones are made of calcium oxalate, so people assume calcium causes them. Research shows a more nuanced picture: getting calcium from food is linked to a *lower* risk of stones, likely because it binds oxalate in the gut. Calcium *supplements*, especially taken without food, have been linked to a modest increase in stone risk in some large studies. Alcohol adds a separate factor, because dehydration concentrates your urine. If you've had stones, talk to your doctor before taking calcium supplements. Our guide to [whether alcohol causes kidney stones](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-cause-kidney-stones) explains the hydration side.

**Heart health.** Some studies have raised the question of whether high-dose calcium supplements might be linked to heart problems, while others have found no link. This is still debated. The practical takeaway most experts share is simple: aim to get most of your calcium from food, and use supplements to fill a real gap rather than taking large doses "just in case."

## Does Milk Before Drinking Help?

You've probably heard that drinking a glass of milk before going out "lines your stomach." Milk doesn't coat your stomach in any protective way. What's true is that **having food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream**, and milk counts as food in that sense, since it contains protein and fat. A proper meal does the job better than a glass of milk alone.

If you like milk or yogurt, having some before or after drinking is a perfectly good way to add calcium to your day. Just don't expect it to keep you from getting drunk or prevent a hangover.

## A Simple Plan for Social Drinkers

If you drink socially and want to look after your calcium and bones, here's a sensible approach:

1. **Hit your daily calcium target with food first.** Two or three servings of dairy or calcium-fortified foods covers most of it.
2. **Supplement only to fill a gap.** If you can't get enough from food, a modest supplement (often 500 mg or less) is reasonable. Take it with a meal.
3. **Don't forget vitamin D and magnesium.** Calcium doesn't work well without them, and drinking can lower both.
4. **Count antacids.** Calcium carbonate antacids add to your daily total.
5. **Space it from your medicines.** Check with a pharmacist if you take antibiotics, thyroid medicine, or osteoporosis drugs.
6. **Keep drinking moderate.** For bones, the amount you drink matters far more than any supplement. Current US guidance is no more than two drinks a day for men and one for women, and less is better.
7. **Do weight-bearing exercise.** Walking, strength training, and similar activities help keep bone strong.

For the habits with the best evidence for feeling better the day after drinking, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take when they drink. It has nothing to do with calcium or bone health, and it won't make up for any of the calcium effects described above. Research on DHM has mostly focused on alcohol metabolism and the liver, and most of it comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising but not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers.

If you'd like to try it, it's generally well tolerated, and it can be taken on the same day as a calcium supplement. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when. If you take prescription medicines, check with your pharmacist before adding any new supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Taking a calcium supplement on a day you drink is generally safe for healthy adults. Take it with food, after you've stopped drinking, and in doses of about 500 mg or less at a time. The bigger issue is what regular heavy drinking does to calcium over the long run: less absorbed, more lost, hormone signals thrown off, and slower bone building. That adds up to weaker bones and more fractures, and calcium pills can't undo it on their own. Get most of your calcium from food, keep vitamin D and magnesium in mind, space calcium away from medicines it interacts with, and keep your drinking moderate. If you're worried about your bones or have symptoms like recurring cramps or tingling, a doctor can check your levels and your bone density.

For how calcium fits with other supplements people take around drinking, see our guides to [milk thistle](/never-hungover/milk-thistle-and-alcohol), and [NAC](/never-hungover/nac-and-alcohol), plus our overview of [the vitamins and minerals alcohol depletes](/never-hungover/vitamins-depleted-by-alcohol).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take calcium with alcohol?**

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no known dangerous reaction between a standard calcium supplement and a few drinks. Take it with food and water after you've stopped drinking, and keep each dose to about 500 mg or less. If you take prescription medicine, have kidney disease, or have had kidney stones, ask your doctor or pharmacist first.

**Does alcohol deplete calcium?**

Heavy drinking does. Alcohol increases calcium loss in urine, can reduce calcium absorption by lowering active vitamin D, disrupts the hormones that control calcium, and drains magnesium, which your body needs to keep calcium levels normal. After one night out the effect is small and temporary. Over years of heavy drinking it contributes to weaker bones.

**Should I take calcium after drinking?**

There's no need to take extra calcium after a night out, and there is no good evidence that calcium helps a hangover. If you already take a daily calcium supplement, it's fine to take it as usual with a meal once you've stopped drinking. A calcium carbonate antacid like Tums can ease heartburn after drinking, but it doesn't treat the hangover itself.

**Does alcohol affect calcium absorption?**

Regular heavy drinking can reduce it. Your gut needs active vitamin D to absorb calcium, and heavy drinking is linked to low vitamin D, liver strain, and damage to the gut lining. Calcium carbonate also needs stomach acid and food to absorb well, so taking it on an empty stomach the morning after drinking means less gets in.

**Can calcium supplements protect my bones if I drink heavily?**

Not on their own. Heavy drinking harms bone in several ways at once, including slower bone building, hormone changes, low vitamin D and magnesium, and more falls. Calcium only addresses one piece. Cutting back on drinking matters far more, and research suggests bone building can start to recover after people stop drinking heavily.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol on calcium channel blockers?**

Calcium channel blockers are blood pressure and heart medicines, like amlodipine and verapamil, and don't contain calcium. Alcohol and these drugs both lower blood pressure, which can cause dizziness or fainting, and verapamil has been reported to slow how fast the body clears alcohol. Ask your doctor or pharmacist how much, if any, alcohol is safe with your specific medicine.

**What are the signs of low calcium from drinking?**

Low blood calcium is uncommon in social drinkers. Signs include tingling around the mouth or in the fingers, muscle cramps or spasms, twitching, fatigue, and confusion. Severe cases can cause an irregular heartbeat or seizures, which need emergency care. Because these overlap with low magnesium, low potassium, and dehydration, a blood test is the only way to know.

**Which calcium supplement is best if I drink?**

Calcium citrate is the more forgiving option if you often take your supplement on an empty or upset stomach, or if you take acid-reducing medicine for reflux, because it absorbs without food. Calcium carbonate is cheaper and works well if you reliably take it with a meal. Many products add vitamin D, which you need to absorb calcium.
